items.title: Allocation Before the Clock: Graph, Set and Game Theory of Professional League of Legends Objective Setups
items.content: arXiv:2610.33626v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Before every neutral objective in professional League of Legends, each team decides which of its five players walk to the pit, which hold a lane, and when to commit. The leading analysis of such setups, TAGNet for Counter-Strike 2, clusters graph-network embeddings of player positions and reads cluster win rates as tactical quality. We treat a setup as an allocation on a walled map: formations are set partitions on the lattice $\Pi_5$, control is a geodesic Voronoi split of a navigation graph, and commitment is an allocation game solved as a quantal response equilibrium priced in win probability. On all 164 games of MSI and Worlds 2025 (2,994 team-setups, minimap tracks validated against Riot positions), trailing teams leave the pit empty far more often than leading teams, by +34.8 percentage points at the first baron and +30.4 percentage points at Atakhan. Our model, HASSE-QRE, finds six setup patterns that whole-model series-bootstrap refits reproduce (ARI 0.819, comparable to 0.813 for TAGNet's $K$-Means step alone) and indicates that teams price fights, travel and committed players, not the objective itself (weight 0.018; fixing it to one costs 59.9 log-likelihood points). The equilibrium reproduces a quarter of the commitment gap, almost all of it through state variables rather than its strategic channels. Weighting a team-level contrast by exposure moves it across $p=0.05$ (0.046 against 0.052). We release the tracks, setups and code.

It finds patterns such as trailing teams leaving objectives unattended. A creative game-theoretic application of AI methods to esports analytics.

items.title: Texture-Aware Strategies for Subregion Style Transfer Augmentation
items.content: arXiv:2610.33910v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A common strategy for data augmentation is to apply style transfer on training images to enrich appearance variations. Recent approaches have combined style augmentation with random erasing by selectively replacing image subregions with style-transferred patches. However, existing methods rely on uniformly random region selection or fixed geometric constraints, which may fail to cover informative texture patterns and limit augmentation diversity. To address these limitations, we propose a texture-aware subregion style augmentation framework that prioritizes regions with strong texture responses for style replacement. Furthermore, we extend this framework with a hybrid region strategy that combines a texture-driven region with an auxiliary random region, implicitly enabling more diverse style perturbations. Experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves higher classification accuracy and improves robustness compared with existing style-based augmentation methods.

items.summary: The paper proposes a texture-aware data augmentation framework that prioritizes image regions with strong texture responses for style-transferred patch replacement, combined with a hybrid strategy mixing texture-driven and random regions. This improves on uniformly random region selection used in prior style-augmentation-plus-erasing methods.
items.reasoning: A reasonable but fairly incremental data augmentation refinement for image classification. The texture-guided region selection is a sensible heuristic, but impact is likely limited to niche benchmark improvements without broader methodological significance.

items.title: On Detection Reliability for Small Object Segmentation
items.content: arXiv:2610.34432v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This study investigates whether predicted bounding boxes are reliable for determining where small-object segmentation should be performed without risking false negatives outside those boxes. The investigation leverages adenovirus particles as small objects, YOLO26x for detection, YO-LO26x-Sem for segmentation, and Mask R-CNN for both detection and segmentation. Segmenta-tion-model predictions were matched to ground-truth adenovirus masks or reference objects using their centroids, with ground-truth mask centroids preferred over ground-truth bounding-box centroids as references for matching. Matched predicted-mask centroids were considered as inside at least one detector-predicted bounding box or outside all such boxes, while ground-truth masks without matched predictions were recorded as having no matched segmentation. For the YOLO26 models, 34 reference objects (47.89%) had matched segmentation centroids inside at least one pre-dicted box, 8 (11.27%) had centroids outside all predicted boxes, and 29 (40.85%) had no matched predicted segmentation. For the Mask R-CNN model, the corresponding counts were 69 (97.18%), 0 (0.00%), and 2 (2.82%). These preliminary experiments demonstrated that restricting segmentation to detector-predicted bounding boxes risks excluding matched segmentation predictions outside those boxes, potentially introducing false negatives.
items.author: Olivier Rukundo
items.summary: Investigates whether predicted bounding boxes reliably indicate where small-object segmentation can be performed without false negatives outside the boxes, using adenovirus particles as test objects and comparing YOLO26x, a semantic variant, and Mask R-CNN. Ground-truth mask centroids are preferred as matching references over box centroids.
items.reasoning: A useful reliability analysis for detection-driven segmentation of tiny objects with relevance to microscopy workflows, but the scope is narrow, evaluated on one object type, and methodologically modest.

Segmenta-tion-model predictions were matched to ground-truth adenovirus masks or reference objects using their centroids, with ground-truth mask centroids preferred over ground-truth bounding-box centroids as references for matching. Matched predicted-mask centroids were considered as inside at least one detector-predicted bounding box or outside all such boxes, while ground-truth masks without matched predictions were recorded as having no matched segmentation. For the YOLO26 models, 34 reference objects (47.89%) had matched segmentation centroids inside at least one pre-dicted box, 8 (11.27%) had centroids outside all predicted boxes, and 29 (40.85%) had no matched predicted segmentation. For the Mask R-CNN model, the corresponding counts were 69 (97.18%), 0 (0.00%), and 2 (2.82%). These preliminary experiments demonstrated that restricting segmentation to detector-predicted bounding boxes risks excluding matched segmentation predictions outside those boxes, potentially introducing false negatives.

items.title: Blendshape Generation for Models with Disconnected Parts: Adding ARKit/MediaPipe Blendshapes to Anime-Style Character Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.35076v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Blendshape generation for 3D models has been extensively researched, but very few works address generating blendshapes for models with multiple disconnected parts. We present a case study of generating fixed facial expression blendshapes for commercial anime-style 3D character models with up to 11 parts per face. To make sure that our system can handle models in a way that is agnostic to topology, we train neural networks to generate deformation fields around the input meshes. We employ at least one network to independently process each part, and the relative positions of their outputs are coordinated by having each network also process the geometry of an anchor part. We use two mechanisms to improve accuracy: having the networks predict whether the output displacement is zero or not, and classifying blendshapes into different size groups and dedicating a network to each group. We also introduce a method to improve blendshape quality by enhancing bilateral symmetry. Our method is simpler than recent neural-network-based works and solves a real problem of the user community of these models.

items.title: MOSHO: A Native Discrete Shark-Inspired Metaheuristic for Hardware-Aware Neural Architecture Search
items.content: arXiv:2610.33358v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Hardware-aware neural architecture search (NAS) requires jointly optimizing predictive accuracy and device-specific latency over discrete search spaces. While multi-objective swarm optimizers show promise, continuous formulations such as the Multi-Objective White Shark Optimizer (MOWSO) can suffer from quantization noise when rounded to integer-encoded architecture vectors. To address this limitation, we propose MOSHO (Multi-Objective Shark Hunting Optimization), a native discrete metaheuristic that replaces continuous motion equations with discrete architecture-editing operators. MOSHO integrates adaptive operator scheduling, energy-regulated restarts, and deferred crowding-distance truncation to enhance exploration and search efficiency. On the merged NAS-Bench-201/HW-NAS-Bench benchmark across 18 contexts, MOSHO achieves a median normalized hypervolume of 0.9987 and IGD+ of 0.0064, yielding Pareto fronts competitive with NSGA-II while reducing search runtime by 96.4% (0.64 s vs. 17.72 s). These results demonstrate that tailored discrete search mechanisms can enable swarm optimizers to achieve high-quality multi-objective solution quality with substantially lower search cost in hardware-aware NAS.

items.title: Designing Customer Feedback for Subscription Boxes
items.content: arXiv:2610.34726v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Problem definition: Subscription box services often ask customers for ratings before choosing what to send. Responses are scarce, and longer questionnaires and finer scales lower completion. We study which candidate items a questionnaire should ask about, and in what format, when the platform then selects a fixed number of them. A design is judged by the expected value lost by not selecting the truly best items. Methodology/results: We approximate each ordinal rating by a Gaussian signal carrying its information at the cutoff between selected and unselected items. As equal numbers of responses per item grow, the ratio of this proxy's loss to the exact loss tends to one. With 1 to 100 responses per item, the two are within about 7 percent. Averaging the information over the prior instead can misstate the loss by about half. For an item far from the cutoff, the value of responses grows slowly at first and then faster, so our envelope rule values responses in blocks. In simulations with a correct prior it lowers the loss by 15 to 81 percent relative to an even spread, and on MovieLens ratings by 6 to 25 percent. Under the proxy, with responses allocated optimally, formats are ranked exactly by one number, the expected information per customer asked. Choosing the format this way comes within about 2 percent of the best on average. Managerial implications: Feedback should go to items whose place in the selection is unclear. Planning helps most when the platform's prior beliefs are informative and right. A platform unsure of its prior should widen it and send the questionnaire in waves. Calibrated on MovieLens ratings, a five-point answer carries about 1.7 times the information of a like/dislike answer, so at equal length the finer scale is better when it cuts completion by less than about 40 percent.
items.author: Renjun Hu, Hyun-Soo Ahn, Stefanus Jasin
items.summary: This operations research paper studies how a subscription box platform should design questionnaires (which items to ask about and in what format) when ratings guide item selection under scarce customer responses. Using a Gaussian-signal approximation to ordinal ratings, the authors derive near-optimal designs whose loss is provably close to the exact optimum. It is a niche but rigorous contribution to information elicitation and survey design.

items.title: Can you Trust Your AI Agent? A Case for AI Loyalty
items.content:
As AI agents become more capable, and as individuals, companies, institutions, and governments come to rely on them for an ever wider range of tasks, the question of whether these agents can be trusted will become increasingly important.

There are two distinct components of agent trustworthiness that are useful to distinguish. The first, which we label loyalty, concerns whether an agent is genuinely attempting to carry out the user's instructions and act in accordance with their interests. The second, which we label reliability, concerns whether an agent is capable enough to accomplish the tasks that we assign to it.

An example of the latter failure (unreliability) would be an agent tasked with maintaining an application accidentally deleting a critical database. Although potentially catastrophic, this failure would stem from an agent's inability to reliably perform its assigned tasks, rather than from any intention to cause harm or undermine the user. By contrast, an example of the former failure (disloyalty) would be an agent tasked with maintaining an application for a company secretly passing sensitive information to a competitor. This failure would not stem from an agent's inability but rather from its willingness to deliberately act against the interests of its user.

As AI agents become more capable, we would expect failures due to unreliability to decrease. Failures due to disloyalty, on the other hand, may become increasingly concerning, since a more sophisticated agent would be better equipped to pursue objectives contrary to their users' interests.

For the purposes of this post, I will concentrate on the question of AI loyalty.

items.title: PoKER: A Probability of Kill Estimation Rate Model for Air-to-Air Missiles Using Machine Learning on Stochastic Targets
items.content: arXiv:2610.32864v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This work introduces PoKER, a novel probabilistic model engineered to optimize missile launch effectiveness in air-to-air scenarios, specifically within Beyond Visual Range (BVR) air combat. Unlike conventional Weapon Engagement Zone (WEZ) models that delineate zones based on static distances such as maximum, minimum, and no-escape ranges, PoKER applies machine learning to predict kill probabilities more accurately by integrating the stochastic behaviors of targets and missile miss distances. This model dynamically evaluates target behavior, greatly expanding the predictive capabilities of engagement analysis. By factoring in elements such as warhead lethality, target and shooter orientations, and the specific conditions of engagement, PoKER provides important insights into engagement dynamics and quantifies success probabilities. Consequently, it can potentially be an important tool for BVR air combat pilots, improving operational decision-making within this specialized combat domain.
items.author: Joao P. A. Dantas, Andre N. Costa, Diego Geraldo, Marcos R. O. A. Maximo, Takashi Yoneyama
items.summary: PoKER is an ML-based probabilistic model that estimates kill probability for beyond-visual-range air-to-air missile engagements, replacing static weapon engagement zone boundaries with dynamic predictions incorporating target stochastic behavior, warhead lethality, and engagement geometry. The work applies machine learning to tactical military decision support.

items.title: From Writing Advice to Manuscript Governance: A Constrained-Transformation Framework for Academic Revision
items.content: arXiv:2610.33001v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Academic revision presents a governance problem when legitimate writing objectives conflict. Writing-process and social-science research show that revision is recursive and that wording carries epistemic and disciplinary commitments. Those literatures identify important constraints but do not settle which objective should prevail when concision, outlet form or stylistic variation conflicts with evidence and claim boundaries. This paper models revision as an admissibility problem under ordered constraints. Task-relative invariants, contextual constraints and mutable presentation choices define the admissible space; a claim-preservation contract links evidence and judgement to an authorised claim boundary. Four governance propositions specify preservation, precedence, context and sufficiency. The Academic Writing Filter implements the model by screening candidate revisions; it is not a universal definition or classifier of good academic writing. The contribution is a technology-independent mechanism for changing presentation without silently changing the research argument.

items.title: Synthetic linguistic data
items.content: arXiv:2610.34215v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Synthetic linguistic data have become increasingly prominent in linguistic research, from the analysis of large collections of AI-generated texts to controlled experiments investigating grammatical and lexical preferences. This glossary entry extends Bresnan's (2016) distinction between the linguistic garden and the bush by introducing an artificial plant nursery as a metaphor for synthetic data. We distinguish between synthetic bush data, consisting primarily of corpus-like collections of model-generated language, and synthetic garden data, in which model outputs are elicited under controlled conditions to investigate specific linguistic hypotheses. We argue that synthetic data constitute a distinct object of linguistic investigation: comparing them with natural language data can reveal both shared patterns and divergences, but their interpretation requires careful consideration of the conditions under which they are generated.

items.title: Adapting LLM-SC to Living Sacred Heritage: Domain-Specific Extraction, Semantic Networks and Human Evaluation on Pashupatinath Temple Reviews
items.content: arXiv:2610.35685v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language model (LLM) pipelines can turn visitor reviews into structured data, but generic schemes may miss rituals, sacred spaces, cultural restrictions and emotionally mixed experiences at living sacred heritage sites. We adapted the LLM-Social Computing (LLM-SC) framework to Pashupatinath Temple, Nepal, by specifying a 12-type entity taxonomy (four original LLM-SC types plus eight sacred-heritage types), four relation types and nine aspect-sentiment dimensions in a GPT-4o extraction prompt, which was applied to a fixed random sample of 2,500 English-language Tripadvisor reviews from a processed corpus of 3,939. The exports contain 11,286 entity, 6,232 aspect-sentiment and 5,590 relation records, covering 2,485, 2,487 and 2,433 reviews, respectively; the eight added sacred-heritage types account for 64.8% of entity records. Against an adjudicated two-annotator reference for 200 reviews, exact normalized surface-and-type matching gave provisional entity scores of 41.0% precision, 21.8% recall and 28.4% micro-F1. Aspect-presence F1 was 53.6% and end-to-end aspect-plus-polarity F1 was 42.6%. Human adjudication supported 153 of 194 first-listed relation candidates (one per review; 78.9%), a candidate-level rate that does not estimate relation recall or whole-graph precision. The contribution is a culturally grounded, domain-specific adaptation with component-wise human evaluation and explicit reproducibility and generalization limitations.

items.summary: Adapts the LLM-Social Computing framework to extract structured entities, relations, and aspect-sentiment from Tripadvisor reviews of Pashupatinath Temple using a custom sacred-heritage taxonomy in a GPT-4o prompt. Produces a large structured dataset (11,286 entity records) with human evaluation and semantic network analysis.
items.reasoning: A well-executed domain adaptation with a useful cultural-heritage dataset, but methodologically incremental — prompt-engineered extraction with a domain taxonomy rather than a new technique.

items.title: Some Memories of Early Anthropic
items.content:
The following events took place between October 2022 and May 2023. I wrote very little of this down at the time so am recalling from memory, and am rendering the gist of the dialogue rather than the exact words used. I’ve also swapped some pronouns and other personal identifiable details.

Please remember that this is not a description of “what Anthropic is like”, but merely the experience of one guy in a junior role during a short window of time, weighted towards emotionally intense moments because they’re easier to remember clearly and because sharing them doesn’t run afoul of the spirit of the confidentiality agreements I signed. Anthropic is now a massive organization with many silos and secrets and I have very little idea what was or is happening there in some overall sense. But given the enormous power of the AI labs and the paucity of public information about their inner workings, I feel compelled to share the most salient parts of my personal experience. I hope this encourages my former colleagues, and folks at other labs, to fill in the rest of the picture.

I’m at the Anthropic office for lunch. The interviews went well. They want me on board. I’m a little unsure. My other offer is a 2-month contract on the OpenAI governance team, working with a friend on some fun conceptual research. I’m leaning towards taking the OpenAI contract - my long-term relationship just ended, I’m still a little burned out from my startup, and the Anthropic job seems potentially quite stressful.

After lunch one of the co-founders pulls me into his office for a wide-ranging, casual chat about how to make AI go well. It’s very fun - he’s smart, personable, funny, urbane. “The government won’t do anything about AI until it’s far too late”, I opine at one point. “Our strategy has to rely on the market and on civil society.”...

items.title: Brute-Force Progress on AlgZoo's 432-param Interpretability Challenge
items.content:
Nick Cammarata's recent article made me want to take a serious stab at interpretability myself. After a bit of consideration, I decided to work on the AlgZoo challenge that was posted here earlier. I trained an estimator on models with the same recipe as the given model. At 20-300 forward passes per network it estimates accuracy with mean squared error 9-36x lower than random sampling, but it's fitted to a population rather than derived, so I don't think it's a breakthrough.

### The challenge

items.title: A Computationally Efficient Non-Interpolation Virtual Trellis Approach for Mammogram Gradient-based Patterns Analysis
items.content: arXiv:2610.34352v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Feature analysis is a crucial step in medical image analysis, particularly in breast cancer classification. Traditional image analysis methods often struggle with optimal patterns along the diagonal axis, computational efficiency and feature buffer storage. Different classical operators require high-efficiency hardware for the complex operations, such as image convolution and gradient analysis, which are used for processing complex machine learning models for training and test operations. Here, in this research, we introduce a non-interpolation virtual trellis-based (NVHT) operator that utilizes a filter kernel over the same square image without transformation to a hexagonal trellis. This proposed method is very efficient in reducing computational and storage costs. The proposed operator is used for improved feature extraction efficiency and accuracy in disease classification. This method outperforms conventional approaches by leveraging a hexagonal pixel representation while maintaining high sensitivity in different directions with less storage.
items.author: Shahid Rasheed, Muhammad Rashid, Seifedine Kadry, Salman A. AlQahtani
items.summary: Introduces NVHT, a non-interpolation virtual trellis operator for extracting gradient-based features from mammograms without transforming images to a hexagonal trellis. The method reduces computational cost and feature buffer storage for breast cancer classification pipelines.

items.title: Resource-Performance Trade-offs in Intra-Aisle Robotic Picking: A Discrete-Event Simulation Comparison of Shuttle Configurations With and Without an Onboard Tote Lift
items.content: arXiv:2610.34708v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This study compares two implemented intra-aisle robotic-picking configurations through discrete-event simulation. Without an onboard tote lift, two level-captive shuttles serve the two tested levels; with the lift, one shuttle remains on its horizontal level and its onboard mechanism moves the order tote to allow picks from the adjacent upper level. Thirty configuration-task-size experiments (n = 1-15 locations; ten replications each) yield 300 replication-level cycle-time observations. Two-sided Welch tests are applied to the replication means, with Holm adjustment across the 15 comparisons. The onboard-tote-lift configuration has longer mean cycle time at all tested task sizes. At n = 15, the means are 299.477 and 333.231 s/cycle, respectively: a 33.753 s increase (11.27%). The corresponding cycle-time-derived item rates are 180.314 and 162.050 items/h (-10.13%). These rates are calculated as 3600n divided by the scenario-mean cycle time; they are not measurements of the combined concurrent capacity of two level-captive shuttles. Importantly, task locations are sampled from different eligible-level sets in the two configurations, so the result concerns the implemented configuration-and-task-generation packages, not the isolated effect of a five-second tote-lift operation under identical picked locations. The study quantifies a cycle-performance difference alongside a reduction from two dedicated shuttles to one within the tested two-level block; it does not quantify system-level maximum throughput, investment cost, or reliability.

items.title: Nonlinear Control of Aerial Manipulator
items.content: arXiv:2610.34454v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This paper presents two controllers for a quadrotor equipped with a two-DOF robot manipulator that physically interacts with the environment. Cartesian impedance and adaptive sliding mode controllers are implemented and compared for a simple hovering task in the presence of some bounded disturbance. A full dynamic model is developed, and the two above controllers are implemented with the same initial conditions and desired position.

items.title: Towards an Architecture-Agnostic Definition of "Attention"
items.content:
This brief post is meant to inspire and to start an open dialogue. I am genuinely curious to listen and incorporate your opinions, challenges, and insights.

# The Context

I have been pondering for some time about the fact that Multi-Layer Perceptrons are known to be universal approximators and good learners, and yet, they are clearly not as useful as Transformers. The general consensus is that it's mostly due to performance limits: that is definitely true, but the explanation never felt satisfactory to me.

Intuition suggests that self-attention enables contextual-based learning, as opposed to memorization-based learning. Until some days ago, I couldn't point my finger to what "contextual" really meant in practice.

The eye opener was this paper, The Bayesian Geometry of Transformer Attention: I am not going to discuss it since that is beyond my competence, but one of its merits is in posing the correct question: can pure in-context learning be identified at all? The authors succeeded in exactly that: they brainstormed a tool called Bayesian wind tunnels, in which learning is possible, but memorization is prohibitively expensive and doesn't improve the learning process.

And they proved exactly what is anecdotically well-known in the ML community: MLPs memorize, while Transformers contextualize.

The paper's findings go well beyond this major insight; however I am going to stop here and, instead, I'll follow a tangential path and pose the next correct question: is attention, in the form of automatic contextualization, something that can be formally defined regardless of the chosen ML architecture?

Let me explain the reason why I am interested into this specific question:...
items.author: Gianluca Calcagni
items.summary: This short LessWrong post explores what makes self-attention more useful than MLPs despite universal approximation, drawing on recent work on Bayesian wind tunnels that separates in-context learning from memorization. The author proposes this as a starting point for an architecture-agnostic definition of attention and explicitly invites community dialogue. It is a conceptual discussion piece rather than original research.
items.reasoning: An earnest and possibly generative conceptual prompt for discussion, but it contains no original experiments or proofs and explicitly defers to others' technical work; value is as a conversation starter.

items.title: Large Language Models: A Plain-Language Overview for Engineers
items.content: arXiv:2610.34585v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are neural networks trained on huge text collections to generate text by predicting what comes next. Engineers using ChatGPT and other generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools need a clear picture of what training changes and prompts add. The article starts with the Transformer, which connects words in context, and pre-training, where models learn to predict text. It then explains how fine-tuning adapts models to requests, with reinforcement learning from human feedback using human answer rankings. Next, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supplies documents, while chain-of-thought prompting encourages intermediate steps and agents use tools. FlashAttention lowers training and running costs by reducing data movement during attention; quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) saves fine-tuning memory. Readers get a life cycle figure and tables comparing methods and their limits. A short checklist for judging LLM evaluation claims flags test material in training (data contamination) and model-based grading (LLM-as-a-judge). It also covers very long inputs (long context) and hallucination, meaning false or unsupported claims. Check factual accuracy separately from whether an answer sounds helpful.
items.author: Bahaeddin T\"urko\u{g}lu
items.summary: A tutorial-style article explaining LLM fundamentals for engineers, covering transformers, pre-training, fine-tuning, RLHF, RAG, chain-of-thought prompting, agents, and efficiency techniques like FlashAttention. It aims to clarify what training versus prompting contributes for practitioners using generative AI tools.

items.title: Wave Is All You Need: A Quantum Language Model Based on Fully Connected Quantum Boltzmann Machine
items.content: arXiv:2610.34492v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This work proposes a self-attention mechanism based on the fully connected quantum Boltzmann machine (FC-QBM), and further constructs a fully connected quantum Boltzmann machine language model (FC-QBM-LM) using the mechanism as the core engine. By performing unitary evolution on semantic quantum states, the mechanism implicitly implements positional encoding and self-attention computation, eliminating the need to decompose continuous semantic streams into discrete matrices for explicit matrix multiplication, with the measurement results naturally satisfying the normalization condition. Specifically, this work rigorously derives the computational principle of the self-attention mechanism based on FC-QBM, and demonstrates that this mechanism is mathematically equivalent to the classical self-attention mechanism. The mathematical principles governing the training and generation of FC-QBM-LM are thoroughly derived, and the two corresponding algorithms are subsequently developed. An 8-qubit FC-QBM-LM is finally constructed and trained on the corpus of Tang poetry. Under the 8-qubit setting, the quantum layer implements the entire positional encoding and self-attention computation pipeline with only 44 parameters. In the noiseless scenario, the model exhibits favorable convergence. Furthermore, the quantum circuit proposed in this work, which terminates with Y-axis rotation gates, achieves better convergence than the counterpart terminating with X-axis rotation gates. Under the small-sample regime and across eight distinct noise intensity levels, the model demonstrates strong noise robustness, retaining over 99% of its noiseless convergence performance. Experiments on five-character quatrain generation reveal that the model preliminarily exhibits three core capabilities: associative and divergent thinking, content generation across imagery and human-aligned word ordering.

items.title: Anthropic are the Good Guys
items.content:
I’m writing these lines in Alamogordo, New Mexico. I’m about as close as a civilian can get to the site of the Trinity test, the first nuclear bomb detonation in history. I fled here from the San Francisco Bay Area; after two weeks of being back I just couldn’t take it anymore. The fear-greed complex that paralyzed me at Anthropic three years ago is now everywhere in the Bay. People are not thinking clearly. Hardly thinking at all, actually. Rumors of astronomical funding rounds and weird financial arrangements and inner ring gossip are everywhere. Everyone is worried. Everyone is checking their phone. Where are we? What’s happening? When did this nightmare start?

In a way I think it started on July 16, 1945, not far from where I’m sitting now. I think it’s impossible to understand Anthropic without putting yourself into the shoes of the Los Alamos physicists huddling together at sunrise in the aftermath of Trinity.

It must have felt like an initiation. An end to childhood, an end to innocence. We can no longer afford to fuck around, those brilliant men must have thought. Unless we figure out how to live peacefully together on this planet, we are all going to die. It’s time to get serious.

And serious we became - we filled endless gray skyscrapers with Very Serious People working at the UN and the EU and the State Department. We tabooed talking in terms of national interest, grounding our values in “human rights” and “benefitting humanity” and respecting the will of the “international community”. I guess it sort of worked, for a while. But it seems that the people who cobbled it together failed to solve the hardest problem of political science: succession. They died a long time ago, and the halls of power are full of scared teenagers in tailored suits pretending to be adults at each other....

items.summary: A reflective essay by a former Anthropic employee, written near the Trinity test site, drawing an analogy between the Los Alamos physicists after the first nuclear detonation and the culture and motivations of Anthropic amid today's frenzied AI race. The piece argues that understanding Anthropic requires grasping the existential dread that shaped its founding culture.

items.title: From Deliberately Constructed Systemic Representations of the World of Activity to Dialogue: A Five-Level Communication Architecture for Strong Language-Based ASI
items.content: arXiv:2610.32869v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper proposes a five-level organization of message formation and understanding within thinking and activity in which ASI participates. Its central thesis is that a language model's context is fundamentally incapable of presenting the foundations of utterance formation for examination and verification. These foundations are established in advance by acquired schemas, systemic representations of the world of activity, and connections accepted as true within them. Neither context nor trained LLM weights, in themselves, attest to the presence of deliberately constructed systemic representations. The five levels distinguish systemic representations of the world of activity, a particular situation cut out from those representations, its narrative description, the full sense of a message, and text. A situation's schema-model is not identical to a story about it. A recipient reconstructs the full sense from an abbreviated text through jointly constructed and agreed-upon representations and joint activity. Reverse work proceeds from the full sense through an extended description and the situation's schema-model to the reconstruction of systemic foundations. The theoretical foundations draw on the systems methodology of G. P. Shchedrovitskiy, the structural differential of A. Korzybski, and the Meaning-Text theory of I. A. Mel'chuk. The contribution is a specific systemic-activity organization of content for examining and adjusting message foundations and controlling the consequences of their transformation. Further research concerns large graphical models of activity on reconstructible systemic foundations, distinct from text generation from context.

It distinguishes systemic representations, situations, narratives, and dialogue levels.

items.title: Data Quality Audit and Bivariate Temperature-Humidity Analysis of a Long-Term LoRaWAN Network: Anomaly Detection, PCA, Clustering and Machine Learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.32438v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Long-term environmental IoT/LPWAN deployments often aggregate heterogeneous data streams from diverse devices without systematic auditing of each variable's actual coverage prior to analysis-an increased risk when multiple sensor types coexist within the same network. This work proposes a C++17 processing pipeline applied to the Tour Perret LoRaWAN dataset (421 937 frames, June 2021--June 2023, 5 devices). A systematic coverage audit integrated into the extraction phase reveals that CO2 is completely missing (0% coverage) and pressure is reported only by an isolated base module (Wyres, 4.24% of the corpus), invalidating the initial hypothesis of a joint four-variable analysis. The analysis is refocused on the Temperature--Humidity pair, jointly available across 205{,}005 frames (95.76%) from 4 Elsys EMS sensors. The pipeline sequentially performs anomaly detection (modified Z-score, Isolation Forest), bivariate Principal Component Analysis, clustering (K-means, DBSCAN), and a multilayer perceptron predicting humidity from temperature and time, whose residuals serve as a detector for slow drift. On real-world data: Temperature--Humidity correlation r=-0.662, two-component PCA (PC1 =83.1% of variance), Isolation Forest detects 2.12% multivariate anomalies while univariate Z-score detects none, calibrated DBSCAN isolates 0.17% noise across 13 clusters, and the MLP achieves $R^2=0.672$ (RMSE =10.54%) in cross-validation. This work demonstrates that per-variable coverage auditing prior to modeling is a necessary methodological step for heterogeneous multi-sensor IoT datasets.

items.content_html: arXiv:2610.32438v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-term environmental IoT/LPWAN deployments often aggregate heterogeneous data streams from diverse devices without systematic auditing of each variable's actual coverage prior to analysis-an increased risk when multiple sensor types coexist within the same network. This work proposes a C++17 processing pipeline applied to the Tour Perret LoRaWAN dataset (421 937 frames, June 2021--June 2023, 5 devices). A systematic coverage audit integrated into the extraction phase reveals that CO2 is completely missing (0% coverage) and pressure is reported only by an isolated base module (Wyres, 4.24% of the corpus), invalidating the initial hypothesis of a joint four-variable analysis. The analysis is refocused on the Temperature--Humidity pair, jointly available across 205{,}005 frames (95.76%) from 4 Elsys EMS sensors. The pipeline sequentially performs anomaly detection (modified Z-score, Isolation Forest), bivariate Principal Component Analysis, clustering (K-means, DBSCAN), and a multilayer perceptron predicting humidity from temperature and time, whose residuals serve as a detector for slow drift. On real-world data: Temperature--Humidity correlation r=-0.662, two-component PCA (PC1 =83.1% of variance), Isolation Forest detects 2.12% multivariate anomalies while univariate Z-score detects none, calibrated DBSCAN isolates 0.17% noise across 13 clusters, and the MLP achieves $R^2=0.672$ (RMSE =10.54%) in cross-validation. This work demonstrates that per-variable coverage auditing prior to modeling is a necessary methodological step for heterogeneous multi-sensor IoT datasets.

items.title: Computer Vision Navigation for an Autonomous Vehicle Model Using Reinforcement Learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.33755v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This work aims to assess the capabilities of the reinforcement learning algorithm, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), in developing a policy capable of controlling the speed and steering angle of a vehicle model to navigate within simulated road lines.   The control system's input is a camera, and its outputs are the rotational speed of the rear wheels and the steering angle of the front wheels, controlling the vehicle's speed and direction, respectively. The algorithm is trained and tested in a simulated environment, where it receives image frames from the vehicle's camera, processes them through a feature extraction algorithm, and feeds them into the policy. For each frame, the policy outputs speed and direction commands for the vehicle. The policy is iteratively updated to enhance its performance.   The reinforcement learning algorithm successfully generates a policy capable of navigating the vehicle in a simplified environment. Potential improvements are suggested to enhance the system's robustness in more complex scenarios.   Creating a simulation environment suitable for testing an advanced reinforcement learning algorithm is a complex task. This project offers a framework for other developers to test different approaches and algorithms. The tested algorithm, PPO, uses proximity intervals - an innovative approach in reinforcement learning. In some scenarios, the algorithm achieved better performance than predecessor algorithms, which are typically harder to implement and require tuning more hyperparameters.

items.title: Trajectory Generation and Control for Quadrotors
items.content: arXiv:2610.34456v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In this project, I explored controller design and trajectory generation for a quadrotor. Differential flatness was used for trajectory generation based on one of the references. A minimum snap trajectory is generated from the given algorithm based on waypoint navigation, and a simple proportional plus derivative (PD) controller is used to track the trajectories. Simulation results are presented which generate smooth trajectories for position and velocity of the quadrotor.

items.summary: Explores controller design and trajectory generation for quadrotors, using differential flatness to produce minimum-snap trajectories through waypoints and a PD controller to track them, with simulation results showing smooth position and velocity profiles. This applies classical techniques from the quadrotor literature rather than proposing new methods.

items.title: Small Groups of Correlated Researchers
items.content:
Summary: The actions taken this decade may be exceptionally important for the future of civilization, but we should be unusually hesitant to proclaim that any course of action is “best.” Still, we should think carefully about what we should do. 

This post was written as part of an introduction to a new reading group I’m starting called “Doing Good in the Age of AGI.” If you want to follow along, the full curriculum can be found here.

## Uncertain in the best of times

Do you think freezing rent prices would be good for the economic middle class? How confident are you? 

You might have an answer that you like, but you’re probably not that confident in it. Perhaps you haven’t formally studied economics, but maybe you’ve had some passing interest in the topic. Ever since Mamdani’s mayoral campaign became a talking point across the country, or since his rent freeze passed in June of 2026, discussion of this economic policy has shifted back into the public spotlight. Maybe you’ve tried to read the arguments on both sides, and you’ve noticed that there’s a lot to read. As it turns out, people are opinionated enough that 82% of renters and homebuyers believe there should be caps on rent increases, but a survey of the top economists shows that only 2%[1] think that rent caps would make the middle class substantially better off over the course of a decade (with some of the disagreement coming from whether or not a benefit would be “substantial”). And within this gap between public sentiment and expert opinion, there is so much discourse and research. The American Economics Association has 23,000 members, about half of which are academics, and a single meta-analysis on rent control reviews over 200 papers....
items.author: Roman Ross
items.summary: Written as an introduction to a new reading group called Doing Good in the Age of AGI, the post reflects on epistemic humility about policy and research priorities, using the example of contested economic policy debates to illustrate correlated errors among small groups of researchers. It argues the community should be cautious about proclaiming any course of action best. It is a reflective essay on community epistemics, not empirical research.

items.title: [Transcript] Kevin Roose does a science communication and AGI sociology in Vox interview
items.content:
This is my second article on journalist coverage of AI and AI safety movements after the HuggingFace incident. The first one was about Garrison Lovely's "Obsolete", and was more of a review. You can read it here.

Kevin Roose, longtime journalist at the New York Times and now cohost of the podcast "Machine Gods" at NPR, has been doing media rounds in support of his new book, "The AGI Chronicles: The Inside Story of the Race to Create an Artificial Superintelligence".

I think it's useful to see what journalist coverage of frontier AI development, the AI safety movement, rationalism and EA looks like after the HuggingFace hack and Jacob Coxon. I've attached the transcript here.

## Intro / Overview

Kevin Roose: 10 years ago, this was crazy. This was considered very much outside the Overton window because the technology of the time wasn't good. It didn't do anything useful. And it was hard to look at a Siri or an Alexa and think this could take over the world. You had to be somewhat odd to find that level of technology threatening. These people who have made all these predictions for a long time about AI becoming powerful and scary have been very vindicated by that belief.

Christine Emba: I'm Christine Emba sitting in for Sean Illing, and this is The Gray Area. My guest today is Kevin Roose, whose new book, "The AGI Chronicles: The Inside Story of the Race to Create an Artificial Superintelligence", came out this October. I'm excited to sit down with an expert, someone who's been following the story from the beginning, to better understand how it all went down and to figure out how scared we should all be. Kevin, welcome to the show.

Roose: Thanks so much for having me.

## What is AGI and who is building it?

Emba: Before we dive in, I think we need to define some terminology for the non-technical listeners. So you use the word "models", you're talking about ChatGPT, but what I guess in a nutshell is AGI? And, explain the core bet of AI to a lay person....

items.title: Making a Custom Mixer Interface for the 1818VSL
items.content:
Now that LLMs have made many kinds of coding a matter of saying what
you're looking for, many more programs make sense.  This weekend it
was audio mixing software, customized for my use case (live sound for
contra dancing) and hardware (a specific obsolete audio interface).

In 2011 PreSonus released
the 1818VSL, an 8-channel audio interface, with low-latency mixing
software.  I wrote:

All I really need is a box with some amplifying inputs that send
tracks from the mic to the laptop and some outputs that let me send
mixes back out again. Then any sort of complex eq, compression, or
other effects can happen in software on the laptop. So I got one: it's
a Presonus AudioBox VSL1818, with eight usable inputs and eight usable
outputs.

At the time I did worry about how long I could expect it to be
supported:

Less future proof. My old board is almost twenty years old and is
still fully compatible with modern gear. In twenty years will I be
able to attach this box to a computer at all?

This was indeed a problem: in order to get the latency down, PreSonus
had written a custom kernel driver.  This integrated very deeply with
the laptop's operating system, so that it could mix and apply effects
as quickly as possible.  In 2015-09, when Apple released OS X 10.11,
they made a ton of changes, including completely rewriting the USB
driver system (IOUSBFamily to IOUSBHost) and adding System Integrity
Protection.  This broke their integration, and PreSonus deprecated
the mixing software.

I was pretty grumpy about this, since this was why I bought it, and fell
back to just using it as an audio interface.

Now that computers will just do things if I explain what I want,
though, it seemed like a good time to pick this back up.  I asked Opus

items.title: At New York Climate Week 2026, MIT connects with a global network
items.content:
Each year, Climate Week NYC brings together more than 100,000 people in more than 1,000 events across the city to discuss climate challenges, explore solutions, and spur action. Participants come from industry, academia, philanthropy, nonprofits, government, and finance and venture capital. And this year, the mix included a strong, cross-campus presence from MIT.

The MIT community could be seen multiple days during Climate Week, with appearances by Evelyn Wang, vice president for energy and climate, at the official opening ceremony discussing artificial intelligence and the climate equation; an event co-hosted by MIT and the Bezos Earth Fund on climate innovation; and 14 sessions organized by the MIT Climate Project and eight MIT departments, labs, centers, and initiatives — including the Abdul Latif Jameel Water and Food Systems Lab (J-WAFS), the MIT Sloan Sustainability Initiative, the Center for Transportation and Logistics (CTL), MIT Lincoln Laboratory, MIT Open Learning, the MIT Initiative for New Manufacturing (INM), the MIT Climate Policy Center, and the Priscilla King Gray (PKG) Center for Social Impact.

“The MIT Climate Project is a whole-of-MIT mobilization, but no single institution can deliver the climate solutions the world needs — from reducing greenhouse gas emissions to adapting to a changing climate and building more-resilient communities and systems,” said Wang, who is also the Ford Professor of Engineering in the Department of Mechanical Engineering. “Climate Week New York is important because it convenes the range of stakeholders and sectors that must work together to confront these challenges. When we connect the MIT community with this global network, we uncover powerful possibilities to strengthen not only our own efforts, but the world’s capacity for change.”

One location, numerous events

Climate Week NYC was held Sept. 21-27 at venues across Manhattan and other New York boroughs. Utilizing multiple spaces at the Dream Downtown Hotel in the Chelsea neighborhood of Manhattan, the MIT coalition attracted more than 700 attendees for events ranging from small, private conversations to workshops and panel presentations.

Larger sessions included “The Future of Data Centers: Technologies to Change the Paradigm.” “Data centers are at an inflection point, facing interconnected technical, operational, economic, and community constraints that demand cross-sector dialogue and innovation,” says Gang Chen, the Carl Richard Soderberg Professor of Power Engineering and faculty director of the Climate Project at MIT.

Chen, who leads the Data Centers of the Future frontier for the Climate Project, convened a panel of experts across research and industry to address technologies that can change the paradigm. “Technology can't solve all the challenges we’re facing with data centers, but technology has a significant role to play in shaping a future role that is more sustainable and better for the communities that are home to these facilities,” Chen says. “This session was a productive conversation on data center challenges and the potential solutions to overcome them.” 

The workshop “Next-Generation Super Pollutant Solutions: Challenges and Opportunities,” hosted by Jesse Kroll, a faculty director and lead for the Super Pollutants frontier for the Climate Project, convened speakers from the Environmental Defense Fund, Spark Climate Solutions, and across MIT labs and initiatives. 

Accounting for nearly half of all global anthropogenic warming to date, super pollutants currently lack viable solutions for adequate abatement. Many super pollutants have shorter atmospheric lifespans than carbon dioxide, with solutions providing an “emergency brake” to decrease peak warming in our lifetimes. Investments in tackling super pollutants can generate economic benefits, including lowering health-care costs and increasing productivity, and require cross-disciplinary teams to develop and advance the next-generation solutions to meaningfully address super pollutant emissions. 

“Super pollutant mitigation is getting a lot of attention as an ‘emergency brake’ for near-term climate warming. But a huge fraction of our super pollutant emissions simply cannot be mitigated with current technologies and approaches,” said Kroll, the Peter de Florez Professor in the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering. “Our session focused on the innovation — technical and otherwise — needed to tackle these hard-to-abate pollutants.”

Other events included:

- “2026 State of Supply Chain Sustainability Report” with the MIT CTL
- “Building Flood Resilience” with MIT Lincoln Laboratory
- “Climate Communication for Impact” from the MIT Climate Project
- “Climate Impact Founder and Funder Connect” with the PKG Center for Social Impact
- “Educating Tomorrow's Climate Leaders: An MIT Perspective” from the MIT Climate Project
- “Trading for Food Security in a Changing Climate” with J-WAFS
- “Industrial Decarbonization: Pathways to Productivity and Growth” with MIT INM
- “Mobilizing Climate Knowledge for Action” with MIT Open Learning
- “Rethinking Climate Innovation” from the MIT Climate Project
- “What is Sectoral Acceleration and How Do We Fund It” with the Sloan Sustainability Initiative

Rethinking the climate innovation pipeline with the Bezos Earth Fund

A critical climate challenge is moving from breakthrough technology to real-world impact at scale. MIT and the Bezos Earth Fund brought together leaders from industry, venture capital, government, academia, philanthropy, and startups to explore solutions for a stronger innovation pipeline. 

A panel of MIT faculty and alumni spinout leaders Asegun Henry, Seonghoon Woo, Ariel Furst, and Assil Halimi, moderated by Ray Rothrock, venture capitalist and life member of the MIT Corporation, explored the period between a promising scientific invention and commercial deployment. For many breakthroughs that can benefit climate and nature, that journey requires more early-stage science and engineering research, specialized testing infrastructure, validation, patient capital, and pathways to demonstration and pilot projects.

“A breakthrough in the lab is not yet impact in the world. For climate and energy technologies, we need to think about the entire journey — from discovery and invention through validation, commercialization, and deployment — and build better pathways through the gaps along the way,” Wang said in a conversation with Tom Taylor, Bezos Earth Fund president and CEO. 

Tapping into global nexus to find and scale solutions

New York Climate Week is a global nexus for climate, where the connections required to develop, test, and scale potential solutions form. Across the board, MIT sessions addressed the need for solutions to be large in magnitude, technically feasible, and contextually realistic. 

 “Even when a technology is low-cost, it doesn’t mean it will diffuse naturally or get widely adopted,” said Claire Walsh, global director of policy and communications at MIT’s Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab. “Frontier technologies are often more expensive to start, so that means it’s even more important for scientists and engineers to think about end user adoption, and their incentives and constraints, from the start.”

  • “What is Sectoral Acceleration and How Do We Fund It” with the Sloan Sustainability Initiative

Rethinking the climate innovation pipeline with the Bezos Earth Fund

A critical climate challenge is moving from breakthrough technology to real-world impact at scale. MIT and the Bezos Earth Fund brought together leaders from industry, venture capital, government, academia, philanthropy, and startups to explore solutions for a stronger innovation pipeline.

A panel of MIT faculty and alumni spinout leaders Asegun Henry, Seonghoon Woo, Ariel Furst, and Assil Halimi, moderated by Ray Rothrock, venture capitalist and life member of the MIT Corporation, explored the period between a promising scientific invention and commercial deployment. For many breakthroughs that can benefit climate and nature, that journey requires more early-stage science and engineering research, specialized testing infrastructure, validation, patient capital, and pathways to demonstration and pilot projects.

“A breakthrough in the lab is not yet impact in the world. For climate and energy technologies, we need to think about the entire journey — from discovery and invention through validation, commercialization, and deployment — and build better pathways through the gaps along the way,” Wang said in a conversation with Tom Taylor, Bezos Earth Fund president and CEO.

Tapping into global nexus to find and scale solutions

New York Climate Week is a global nexus for climate, where the connections required to develop, test, and scale potential solutions form. Across the board, MIT sessions addressed the need for solutions to be large in magnitude, technically feasible, and contextually realistic.

“Even when a technology is low-cost, it doesn’t mean it will diffuse naturally or get widely adopted,” said Claire Walsh, global director of policy and communications at MIT’s Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab. “Frontier technologies are often more expensive to start, so that means it’s even more important for scientists and engineers to think about end user adoption, and their incentives and constraints, from the start.”

Over the last few months I have been on a voyage of discovery, finding that my previous assumptions about political coalitions and ideologies no longer hold. The ground is shifting beneath our feet. It is AI which has made this apparent.

- Hangouts: Holistic meditation centers, crystal shops

- Politics: Illuminati lizard theory, default mainstream views, aggressively apathetic ("this whole plane of existence is an illusion, maaaan")

- Favorite drugs: psychedelics, nootropics

- Diet: organic non-GMO, health-oriented vegetarian, "The [Name] Diet"

- Religion: All religions contain a kernel of truth

- AI: Yes

Pink-Haired Commie Poetry Slam Tribe:

- Hangouts: Various bookstores

- Occupation: "artist", barista (but secretly an artist), community college adjunct, unemployed(?) (it's hard to tell because they don't usually bring up their job in conversation)

- Politics: Far-left, socialist/communist ("Democrat party is fascist, revolution now")

- Favorite drugs: marijuana, cheap alcohol

- Diet: some animal-rights-oriented vegetarian, otherwise junk food / dumpster diving

- Religion: Mainline Protestant, militant atheism

- AI: No...

items.title: Hair Thickness of My Friends
items.content:
# Intro

I have a microscope. It can see hair.

Humans have hair. Some of my friends are humans.

How thick is my friends' hair?

Apparently, if I go around asking my friends for a strand of their hair, about half will just give one to me, and almost all the rest will give one when I explain that I'm going to see how thick it is under a microscope. Your mileage may vary.

My parents have not yet chanced upon the card with taped and labelled hair strands, but if they do then they might have some, uh, pointed questions. I'll just tell them I'm trying to diversify my clone army.

Hey, at least it's not like that time a friend of a friend's ex once drew someone's blood at a party.[1] Unfortunately, I never got around to asking her for one of the blood vials she was known to possess.

# Methods

To measure length, I broke off a tiny piece of a clear ruler and put it under the microscope with the hair. Then, I had Free Claude (from 2025?) write some code so I could compare two lengths easily by clicking points. Then I modified some Claude analysis code because I was too lazy to write it myself.

Here's what mine looked like (At the time I had some black hair and some bleached bronze-ish hair, and both seemed about as thick, so I just used the latter):

The reference is 1 mm, so my hair was about 85 microns thick.

# Results

Here's an anonymized bar plot, where my id is 16. Id 5 and id 6 come from the same person, but the 6th was a sample of hair dyed red and the 5th was of black hair. The colors are according to biological sex (most are trans women because friendship selection pressures):

The mean's 78 microns and the (Bessel corrected) sd's 12. That's in line with this international study[2] (I live in America and most participants were some flavor of white):

And look, 5/16 or about 31% of my victims subjects are outside of one sd of the mean, and 1/16 or about 6% got quite close to two sds. I guess the statisticians weren't lying after all!...
